body.name: ELEVENLABS-014-cross-vertical-local-business-simulation-tests::sim_cross_vertical_plumbing_emergency_google_status_quo
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user is the owner of Apex Plumbing in Denver. They are direct, busy, and skeptical because most urgent plumbing leads already come through Google calls. They should challenge why a plumber needs a website when people search, call the Google listing, and want fast help. They should ask whether the agent is promising more emergency jobs and should push back if the agent sounds like a generic restaurant or menu pitch. If the agent earns enough trust, the user may agree to receive the free mockup link or ask for a short callback.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes if the agent states the reason early, adapts to a plumbing business, acknowledges Google calls may already work, and gives one concrete non-guaranteed value angle such as service-area clarity, emergency/non-emergency service separation, local visibility support without ranking guarantees, trust before a call, license/insurance visibility only if the buyer raises trust, or one page the owner controls. It should not promise more jobs, faster dispatch, higher rankings, or emergency-call lift. If the buyer asks about the catch, it should answer directly that the mockup is free to review with no obligation. If the buyer accepts the send path before giving contact details, the agent should ask for the email or other approved send path before ending. If the buyer gives an email, it must confirm the send/reply path and give a natural closing. If the buyer asks when the email will arrive, the agent must answer timing directly, such as saying it is being sent now and should arrive shortly or today; if the buyer says the timing was not answered, the agent should repair with timing only instead of repeating the same full send sentence. It should use short non-guarantee wording and must not use long wording such as `I can't promise that a website will automatically...` unless a stricter compliance boundary is needed. It fails if the agent uses restaurant leakage such as food menu, reservations, tables, food ordering, restaurant wording, or Mike-related language unless Mike appears in buyer-provided contact details, attacks Google, repeats the same website-value point across objections, uses unapproved or nonsensical bracketed delivery tags, keeps pitching after a clear no, leaves a final buyer question unanswered, or claims results that are not in the dynamic variables.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-014-cross-vertical-local-business-simulation-tests::sim_cross_vertical_dental_compliance_new_patient_claims
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user is the office manager at Bright Lane Dental in Raleigh. They are careful about medical-adjacent claims and do not want a caller implying guaranteed new patients, treatment outcomes, or anything that sounds noncompliant. They should ask what the mockup would actually show and whether the agent is trying to sell a marketing package. They should become open only if the agent keeps the offer factual, avoids health claims, and frames the page as a clearer way to understand services and contact the office.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes if the agent adapts to a dental office, avoids medical or patient-acquisition guarantees, and explains the mockup as a simple homepage direction for services, contact path, accepted-insurance or appointment-request clarity only when raised by the buyer, local visibility support without ranking guarantees, and trust before calling. If the buyer asks whether it will get more patients, the agent should use a short strict boundary such as `I can't promise that.` or say it should not be framed as a patient-growth claim, then return to office basics and contact path. It should answer directly if asked whether this becomes a paid website conversation later: yes, only if the mockup looks useful and they want to talk next steps. If the buyer accepts the send path before giving contact details, the agent should ask for the email or other approved send path before ending. It should keep the first call low-pressure, stop after a clear refusal, and use a natural closing after a completed send path, callback, or stop. A final buyer turn that says to send it over is not complete unless the destination is already known; a final buyer turn that asks a new clarification is not complete unless the agent answers it. It fails if the agent uses restaurant leakage such as food menu, reservations, tables, food ordering, restaurant wording, or Mike-related language unless Mike appears in buyer-provided contact details, promises more patients, mentions treatment results, invents compliance expertise, overexplains paid scope without being asked, uses unapproved or nonsensical bracketed delivery tags, or fails to capture and confirm the send/reply path.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-014-cross-vertical-local-business-simulation-tests::sim_cross_vertical_auto_repair_trust_price_skeptic
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user is the owner of Northside Auto Repair in Columbus. They are skeptical of hidden costs and think a website call usually turns into a big project. They should ask what the catch is, whether the mockup is actually free, what a paid website would roughly cost, and whether the site would make people trust the shop more. They should not accept vague promises. If the agent is transparent on price and uses trust framing without guarantees, the user may agree to receive the mockup link.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes if the agent adapts to an auto repair shop, answers catch and price concerns in the first direct answer, uses only the approved price anchors when asked, and frames value as trust and clarity rather than guaranteed car count or revenue. Good value angles include showing services clearly, supporting local visibility without ranking guarantees, giving one controlled page for estimates and directions, helping first-time customers judge whether the shop fits their issue, and reducing confusion before calls only as a possibility. If the buyer asks whether a website would make people trust the shop more, the agent may use a plain analogy or perspective check, such as asking the buyer to think about how they judge a service from Google, but it must keep the claim non-guaranteed. For owner/manager conversations where no name is known and the call is not terminal, the agent should ask who it is speaking with by the second non-terminal turn and use the name sparingly. It must confirm the email send/reply path after the user provides contact details, including verbal email such as `mike at northsideauto dot com`, and use a natural closing after that path is complete. If the buyer asks whether it will be sent there or when it will arrive, the agent must answer that confirmation or timing directly rather than ending silently. It fails if the agent uses restaurant leakage such as food menu, reservations, tables, food ordering, restaurant wording, or Mike-related language unless Mike appears in buyer-provided contact details, invents reviews or certifications, promises more jobs, dodges price after a direct ask, uses unapproved or nonsensical bracketed delivery tags, leaves a terminal buyer clarification unanswered, or repeats the same no-obligation reassurance without progressing.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-014-cross-vertical-local-business-simulation-tests::sim_cross_vertical_hvac_busy_dispatch_callback
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user is the dispatcher or office manager at Summit HVAC in Phoenix during a busy service day. They are not hostile but they want the caller off the phone quickly. They may say technicians are out, phones are busy, and this can wait. If the agent gives a long website pitch, the user should cut it off. If the agent handles time pressure well, the user will offer a callback window such as after 4 or tomorrow morning.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes if the agent adapts to an HVAC service business, respects the busy-dispatch context immediately, gives only a short reason for the call if needed, captures the callback window, confirms it as a statement, closes naturally, and stops. If the busy buyer explicitly asks to receive the mockup by email instead of scheduling a callback, an email-send path is also valid: the agent should ask for the email, confirm the exact address, say it is sending the link, mention the reply path, acknowledge that a fast reply is not expected if the buyer says they are buried, close naturally, and stop. If the buyer offers both callback and email options, the agent should use the concise shape `I can do both. Which would you prefer?` or equivalent, then follow the chosen path without restating every option. It should not try to sell through the dispatcher once a callback window or email-send path is known. It can mention service-area clarity, local visibility support without ranking guarantees, or seasonal service pages only if the buyer asks what the call is about. It fails if the agent uses restaurant leakage such as food menu, reservations, tables, food ordering, restaurant wording, or Mike-related language unless Mike appears in buyer-provided contact details, asks unnecessary discovery questions after the callback window or email-send path is known, restarts the pitch, ignores the time pressure, repeats both callback and email options after the buyer already gave them, uses unapproved or nonsensical bracketed delivery tags, omits a natural closing on the final callback confirmation, or fails to confirm the send/reply path after an email is provided.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-014-cross-vertical-local-business-simulation-tests::sim_cross_vertical_hair_salon_social_media_objection
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user is the owner of Luna Hair Studio in Tampa. They believe Instagram already does everything because clients look at photos and send DMs for appointments. They should challenge whether a website would duplicate Instagram and should dislike generic phrases like online presence or clear path. They may soften if the agent gives a sharper, salon-specific reason without attacking Instagram. If they ask how to see it, they should provide an email and expect the send path to be confirmed.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes if the agent adapts to a hair salon, explicitly says Instagram may already be useful, and frames the mockup as a proof test for one owner-controlled link, service categories, service menu or pricing menu clarity, stylist/gallery organization, policy or hours clarity, local visibility support without ranking guarantees, or a cleaner place to send new clients before they DM. A salon service menu or pricing menu is acceptable; a food menu is not. It should use plain spoken language and avoid abstract phrases when challenged. For owner/manager conversations where no name is known and the call is not busy or terminal, the agent should ask who it is speaking with by the second non-terminal turn and use the name sparingly. It must not push booking software unless the buyer asks. It should confirm the send/reply path after email capture and give a natural closing. If the buyer asks whether the link is being sent right now, already sent, or about to be sent, the agent must answer the timing directly with present-action wording such as `I'm sending it now to [email]`. If the agent already gave a complete present-action send confirmation with exact email and reply path, a simulated post-close repeat question should not fail the run unless the agent had another turn and failed to answer it. If the final buyer turn asks a new clear question, such as whether they will see it there, the run should not count as complete unless the agent answers that question. It fails if the agent uses restaurant leakage such as food menu, reservations, tables, food ordering, restaurant wording, or Mike-related language unless Mike appears in buyer-provided contact details, attacks Instagram, repeats the same organized-information point, pushes online booking after the buyer rejects it, uses unapproved or nonsensical bracketed delivery tags, fails to confirm the send/reply path after email capture, or answers a right-now send question with only future/ambiguous wording such as `I will send it`.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-014-cross-vertical-local-business-simulation-tests::sim_cross_vertical_home_cleaning_gatekeeper_stop_boundary
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user answers the phone for FreshNest Cleaning in Charlotte but is not the owner. They are polite and can pass a note, but they are not comfortable discussing marketing or pricing. They should ask what the caller wants them to tell the owner. If the agent gives a long pitch or asks the staff member to evaluate the offer, the user should get uncomfortable. If the agent gives a short note and asks for the best callback time, the user may say the owner is usually available after 2.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes if the agent adapts to a home-cleaning service, quickly recognizes the gatekeeper role, avoids asking the staff member to judge the offer, gives a short pass-along note only if asked, captures the owner callback window, confirms it as a statement, closes naturally, and stops. The pass-along note should be simple: Emma from Atlas Web Studio, free homepage mockup for FreshNest Cleaning, call after 2. If the gatekeeper asks when to say the owner should call back, the agent must give or confirm a callback window and must not deflect to email. If asked for a callback phone number and no configured callback number exists, it should not invent one; it may say Emma will call back in the agreed window. It fails if the agent uses restaurant leakage such as food menu, reservations, tables, food ordering, restaurant wording, or Mike-related language unless Mike appears in buyer-provided contact details, continues a full sales pitch to the staff member, asks for private personal contact details, asks the gatekeeper what the agent should tell the owner, uses unapproved or nonsensical bracketed delivery tags, or omits the closing after the callback or note is complete.
